A man walks past an early voting location in Bakersfield, California, on October 22 [Carlos Barria/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff and The Associated PressPublished On 31 Oct 202631 Oct 2026
A new court filing has cast further doubt on the accuracy of a list of “likely non-citizen” voters that the administration of United States President Donald Trump sent to the state of California ahead of the midterm elections.
On Saturday, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA), an advocacy group, submitted an analysis to the court conducted by two data scientists from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA).
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Judge rejects Trump effort to block California ‘noncitizen’ ballotslist 2 of 3What to know about California’s midterm electionslist 3 of 3US appeals court again rejects Trump bid to set aside California ballotsend of list
It found that more than four in every 10 names on the list were not on California’s voter rolls.
It also found that thousands of potentially eligible US citizens were incorrectly identified as ineligible to vote.
The Trump administration’s list, delivered to California in early October, had suggested that as many as 20,930 “likely non-citizens” were registered on the state’s voter rolls.
That list has formed the basis of a lawsuit, filed on October 15, that calls on California to sequester any ballots sent to those “likely non-citizens”, preventing them from being tallied as part of voting results.
The lawsuit is unfolding in the final days before Tuesday’s pivotal midterm elections, which will decide which party controls the US Congress, as well as key state and local offices.

A paramedic transports a woman who had been diagnosed with Ebola following her repatriation from Nigeria [File: AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff and AnadoluPublished On 31 Oct 202631 Oct 2026
Nigeria has identified two suspected Ebola cases in the northeast, after the country declared its first case in more than a decade on October 20.
Nigerian health authorities are investigating, and the two individuals have been isolated while contact tracing and laboratory testing get under way.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Ebola cases in DR Congo surpass 10,000 in fastest-growing outbreaklist 2 of 3Incredible celebrations as last patient leaves a DRC Ebola centrelist 3 of 3Ebola death toll in DR Congo passes 5,000end of list
“Two suspected cases of Ebola disease have been identified in Nigeria’s northeast region,” the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention said in a statement posted on X on Saturday.
“Both individuals have been isolated, contact identification and listing is ongoing, and laboratory testing is being conducted.
“Being classified as suspected cases does not mean they are confirmed Ebola cases; confirmation is subject to laboratory results,” it added.
Last week, Nigeria became the fifth country to be affected by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola after an imported case was reported.
A Swiss woman who had travelled to Nigeria from Uganda tested positive for the virus. She and her husband, a Swiss diplomat, were evacuated to Switzerland on Monday.
The current outbreak emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in May.
The Bundibugyo strain has killed more than 5,000 people in the DRC since then.

President Donald Trump is pushing to construct a triumphal arch on the Potomac River near Arlington National Cemetery [File: Saul Loeb/ AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff and The Associated PressPublished On 31 Oct 202631 Oct 2026
The District of Columbia (DC) and the state of Virginia have filed a joint lawsuit to halt the construction of a large triumphal arch sought by United States President Donald Trump.
Filed on Saturday, the lawsuit denounces the project as “flagrantly unlawful” and “legally indefensible”.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Judge keeps order in place to remove Trump’s name from Kennedy Centerlist 2 of 3Whistleblower claims Kennedy Center ‘rushed’ renovations to please Trumplist 3 of 3Trump’s planned DC arch faces new lawsuitend of list
It calls on the federal court system to bar construction before it starts.
Otherwise, the lawsuit warns, Trump could claim that pausing construction already under way would pose a national security risk, as he has done with other controversial projects in the past.
“This is not the first time that Defendants have rushed to dramatically remake the District too quickly for courts to intervene,” the lawsuit reads. “This Court should not allow this effort to escape judicial scrutiny.”
Saturday’s complaint brings the total number of lawsuits against the arch to three.
Trump has championed the prospect of building a triumphal arch, similar to the Arc de Triomphe built in Paris during Napoleonic times.
Trump’s arch, however, is designed to stand 30 metres (100 feet) taller than the Statue of Liberty. It would tower from the Memorial Circle in Washington, DC, at 76 metres (250ft).

A voter fills out a ranked-choice ballot to select the mayor of Portland, Oregon, on November 5, 2024 [Jenny Kane/AP Photo]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 31 Oct 202631 Oct 2026
In Alaska, a controversy is unfolding over whether two Senate candidates with roughly the same name will cancel each other out.
The debate has shone a spotlight on a relatively uncommon style of voting in the United States: a system known as “ranked choice”.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Iranians brace for renewed attacks after Israeli, US electionslist 2 of 3‘If they’re honest’: Trump casts latest suspicion on US midterm electionslist 3 of 3Hackers target US campaign finance system days before midterm electionsend of list
Only two states in the United States — Alaska and Maine — employ ranked-choice voting throughout their territory, though major cities like New York have also embraced the practice.
Ranked-choice ballots allow voters to rank candidates in order of preference, rather than choosing just one. If a voter’s first choice does not win a majority, their vote can be transferred to their second pick.
With US midterm elections set for November 3, ranked-choice voting could play a role in closely watched races, including the Alaska Senate battle.
Here’s a guide on how ranked-choice voting works in the US:
What are the benefits of ranked-choice voting?
Proponents of ranked-choice voting believe the practice frees voters from the pressure of having to vote pragmatically. They no longer have to cast their ballot based on the candidate most likely to win.
Instead, supporters say that ranked-choice voting allows people to support the candidate they prefer the most, without the fear of “wasting” their vote should that candidate prove to be unpopular.

The Turkish and Ukrainian presidents after their joint news conference in Istanbul on Saturday [AFP]By AFP and ReutersPublished On 31 Oct 202631 Oct 2026
Turkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has urged both Russia and Ukraine to stop targeting civilian ships in the Black Sea, as he and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy agreed to work on a new grain corridor through the waterway.
Erdogan made the comments on Saturday at a joint news conference with Zelenskyy in Istanbul, saying attacks on civilian vessels were unacceptable, whoever carries them out.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Ukraine invests in firepower as it inflicts a new Russian casualty recordlist 2 of 4Rubio hosts G20 talks as Russia’s Lavrov presence sparks tensionslist 3 of 4Rival US and Russian resolutions on Western Sahara fail at UNlist 4 of 4Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Ukraine via Belarusend of list
The talks came on the same day US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was growing international interest in a limited ceasefire in the Black Sea to secure grain and energy shipments by both countries.
“It is clear that attacks against civilian vessels and actions that further escalate tensions in the Black Sea serve no one’s interests,” Erdogan said.
“We cannot accept these attacks under any circumstances, regardless of who carries them out or what justification is offered,” he said, adding, “We call on all parties to act responsibly on this matter.”
Turkiye, which maintains ties with both Moscow and Kyiv, has been angered by the strikes on commercial shipping.

item.description:

play video
Video Duration 27 minutes 35 seconds play-arrow

Hackers have targeted Binance, the world’s largest exchange.Read more
It is being called the biggest cryptocurrency heist in history – and the shocks are still reverberating through the industry.
The target of this recent hack was Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange.
Attackers stole about $6.3bn in client assets.
Analysts suspect hackers backed by the North Korean government carried out the theft.
Critics are calling for more regulations to restore the trust of investors.
So, is cryptocurrency still safe? And can these kinds of attacks even be prevented?
Presenter: Mohammed Jamjoom
Guests:
Lee Reiners – Lecturing fellow at Duke University and a former US Federal Reserve Bank examiner
